name: Kumasi Ghost
description: The Kumasi Ghost is a specialized ancestral spirit from the Ashanti tradition of Ghana, particularly associated with the royal court of Kumasi, the historic capital of the Ashanti Kingdom. These spirits serve as messengers and intermediaries between the living world and the ancestral realm, playing a crucial role in the spiritual governance of the Ashanti people. The Kumasi Ghost is distinct from ordinary ghosts or wandering spirits because it is specifically connected to the royal court, carrying messages between the living king and the departed kings who sit in the ancestral council. The belief in these spirits reflects the Ashanti understanding that the living and the dead exist in a continuous relationship of mutual obligation, with the ancestors retaining an active interest in the affairs of their descendants and the health of the kingdom
source: Regional survey of West African oral traditions — Yoruba, Akan, Mande, Igbo, Ewe, and related peoples as documented by Herskovits, Frobenius, Parrinder, and ethnographic surveys.

name: Kumbhakarna (Sleeping Giant)
description: Kumbhakarna is a powerful rakshasa and the younger brother of Ravana from the Hindu epic Ramayana. Despite his gigantic size and enormous appetite, he is described as a virtuous character and a great warrior. He was born with immense strength, having subdued both Indra and Yama. Fearing his power, Indra manipulated Brahma to curse Kumbhakarna to sleep like the dead. At Ravana's plea, the curse was commuted so Kumbhakarna sleeps for six months and wakes for six months. During his waking period, he wreaks havoc and devours to his heart's content. In the Bhagavata Purana, he is said to be the incarnation of the gatekeeper deity Vijaya, who was sentenced to three mortal lifetimes. Along with his brother Jaya (who became Ravana), Vijaya became Kumbhakarna in his second incarnation. He fought valiantly in the war against Rama, destroying 8,000 vanaras before being slain by Rama's Indrastra arrow, which decapitated him. Despite knowing Rama was divine, he fought out of loyalty and dharma to his brother and kingdom
source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bhagavata Purana, Kamba Ramayanam, Hindu mythology

name: Kumiho
description: The Kumiho is a nine-tailed fox from Korean folklore, a powerful and complex supernatural being that shares characteristics with the Japanese kitsune and Chinese huli jing but possesses distinctively Korean attributes. Unlike its Japanese counterpart, the kumiho is almost always a malevolent or tragic figure, a cursed being that must consume human hearts or life essence to survive or to achieve its goal of becoming fully human. The kumiho is typically depicted as a beautiful woman who uses her appearance to seduce men, but unlike the playful or benevolent fox spirits of other traditions, the Korean nine-tailed fox is driven by hunger, curse, or an obsessive desire for humanity. The kumiho legend explores themes of identity, transformation, and the cost of becoming something one is not, making her a more tragic and ambiguous figure than her foreign cousins
source: Korean folklore, Samguk Yusa

name: Kumvo
description: Kumvo is a spirit being from the mythology of the Kwakiutl people, also known as the Kwakwaka_wakw, an Indigenous nation of the Pacific Northwest coast of Canada. These spirits inhabit the rich spiritual landscape of Kwakiutl tradition, where the natural and supernatural worlds are deeply intertwined and where animals, natural features, and ancestral spirits all possess consciousness and power. The kumvo is part of the complex Kwakiutl understanding of the spirit world, which includes numerous categories of beings from animal spirits and ancestor spirits to the powerful beings that appear in the winter ceremonials. The Kwakiutl spiritual tradition is one of the most elaborate among Northwest Coast peoples, with an extensive pantheon of supernatural beings that govern all aspects of life. The kumvo would have been understood through the oral traditions passed down by elders and through the ceremonial life of the community
source: Indigenous Canadian folklore — spirit documented in First Nations oral tradition.

name: Kuntilanak
description: Kuntilanak is a female vampire spirit from Indonesian and Malay folklore, one of the most feared supernatural beings in Southeast Asia. She is the ghost of a woman who died during childbirth or as a virgin, condemned to wander the earth in torment. The kuntilanak shares characteristics with the similar pontianak spirit of Malay tradition, and the names are sometimes used interchangeably across the region. She is a vengeful spirit who targets pregnant women and newborn infants, driven by jealousy and the tragedy of her own unfinished life. The kuntilanak legend is deeply embedded in Indonesian culture, appearing in countless folk tales, films, and urban legends. Unlike many supernatural beings that are purely malevolent, the kuntilanak is sometimes portrayed with tragic depth, a spirit whose evil actions stem from the injustice of her death and the impossibility of finding peace
source: Indonesia mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Kupua
description: Kupua are shapeshifting spirits from Hawaiian folklore, powerful supernatural beings that can take the form of any animal, plant, or object in the natural world. These spirits are among the most versatile and dangerous entities in the Hawaiian spiritual tradition, capable of moving unseen through the islands and causing harm or help depending on their nature and intentions. The kupua are associated with dark magic and are often summoned or controlled by kahuna sorcerers for specific purposes. However, not all kupua are malevolent; some are neutral or even helpful, serving as guardians of specific locations or families. The concept of kupua reflects the Hawaiian understanding of a universe where the boundaries between different forms of existence are fluid and where spiritual power can be channeled through proper ritual and knowledge. Kupua are particularly active during twilight hours when the veil between worlds is thin
source: Hawaiian mythology — Kupua are shapeshifter demigods documented in Hawaiian oral tradition.

name: Shahmaran (Kurdish Serpent Queen of Wisdom)
description: Shahmaran is a legendary half-woman, half-serpent figure in Kurdish, Turkish, Persian, and Mesopotamian folklore. The name means 'King of the Serpents' in Persian. According to legend, a young man named Camsab accidentally discovered the underground realm of the serpents, where Shahmaran (the beautiful serpent queen) ruled. She shared her wisdom with him. When Camsab was forced to reveal her location to a tyrannical vizier, Shahmaran accepted her fate. She told Camsab that bathing in her boiled flesh would grant immortality to the vizier, but the first sip would kill him. Camsab tricked the vizier, who drank first and died. Camsab bathed and became immortal. Her spirit lives in the city of Tarsus and in Kurdish cities like Mardin and Diyarbakır. Shahmaran is a symbol of hidden wisdom, secret knowledge, and female power
source: Kurdish oral tradition, Turkish and Persian folklore, Mesopotamian mythology

name: Kurupira
description: Kurupira is a forest spirit from the folklore of Uruguay and the Guarani-speaking regions of South America, a wild and fearsome creature that dwells in the deepest parts of the forest as the lord of all woodland animals. This short, ugly, hairy being is the undisputed master of the wilderness, commanding the animals and plants of the forest according to its will. The kurupira is one of the most important nature spirits in Guarani tradition, serving as both protector of the forest and punisher of those who harm it. Hunters and woodcutters must obtain the kurupira permission before taking anything from the forest, or they risk its terrible wrath. The spirit is particularly associated with the protection of pregnant women and children who become lost in the woods, though its methods of protection are often violent and terrifying to those who do not understand its motives
source: Uruguay mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Kushtaka
description: The Kushtaka, meaning "Land Otter Man" in the Tlingit language, is a shape-shifting creature from the folklore of the Tlingit and Haida peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast of North America. These are hybrid beings with both otter and human characteristics, created when humans are captured and transformed by the Land Otter spirits that inhabit the dense coastal forests. The Kushtaka are among the most complex supernatural beings in Northwest Coast mythology, possessing a deeply dual nature that makes them both terrifying and benevolent, depending on the circumstances. They are closely associated with the boundary between land and sea, between the human world and the spirit world, and between life and death. The belief in Kushtaka reflects the rich spiritual ecology of the Pacific Northwest, where every animal, natural feature, and atmospheric phenomenon possesses spiritual significance and power
source: Tlingit spiritual tradition; documented in Northwest Coast records.

name: Kuveni (Yakshini Queen of Lanka)
description: Kuveni (also known as Kuvanna or Sesapati) was a Yakshini (demoness) queen ruling in Lanka when Prince Vijaya arrived from India. According to the Mahavamsa, the ancient Pali chronicle of Sri Lanka, she was a shape-shifting demoness who could assume the form of a beautiful sixteen-year-old maiden. She initially imprisoned Vijaya's men through magical means, but when Vijaya overpowered her, she swore loyalty and helped him conquer the Yakkha city of Sirisavatthu. She bore him two children, Jivahatta and Disala. After establishing the Sinhala kingdom, Vijaya repudiated her saying 'men fear superhuman beings' and sent her away to marry a Pandyan princess instead. When Kuveni returned to her own people, they killed her as a traitor for helping the human invaders. Her children fled to the wilderness of Sumanakuta (Adam's Peak), where they married each other and became the ancestors of the Vedda people, Sri Lanka's indigenous inhabitants. The Vedda venerate her as Maha Loku Kiriammaleththo ('Great Elder Sister')
source: Mahavamsa, Dipavamsa, Vedda oral traditions, Seligmann's 'The Veddas'

name: Kvernknurr
description: Kvernknurr (also kvernknarr) is a malevolent mill spirit in Norwegian folklore, particularly associated with the water-powered mills of Vestlandet's waterfall-rich valleys. The kvernknurr lives in mill streams and has an enormous gaping mouth — its upper jaw touches the door beam while its lower jaw rests on the threshold of the mill door. When the mill is grinding, the kvernknurr grips the mill wheel mechanism to stop it, causing the millstones to grind slowly or halt entirely. The only remedy is to shoot a gun into the mill race or throw a knife over the mill house. Unlike the fossegrim who is musical and can be placated with offerings, the kvernknurr is purely malicious and delights in ruining the miller's work. The name comes from kvern (millstone/grind) and knurre (to growl or grumble). Closely related to the kvarnvätten of Swedish folklore
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Kvitormen
description: Kvitormen (the White Serpent) is a magical white snake from the folk belief of Vest-Agder in Sørlandet, particularly the areas of Lyngdal, Bjelland, and Lindesnes. According to tradition, if one could capture a white serpent and place it under the skin of one's arm, the snake would grant supernatural wisdom and healing powers. The person would gain the ability to understand the language of animals, see hidden things, and heal sickness with a touch. However, the white serpent was almost impossible to catch — it was extremely fast, could disappear into the ground, and was protected by supernatural forces. If the white serpent was lost or killed after being implanted, the person would die. The tradition was collected by folklorist Joh. Storaker in the 1800s, who recorded seven variants from Vest-Agder. The white serpent also granted its bearer the ability to find hidden treasure and predict the future
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: La Diablesse (The Devil Woman of the Road)
description: La Diablesse (French for the she-devil) is a seductive yet deadly spirit in Trinidadian and West Indian folklore. She appears as a breathtakingly beautiful woman -- usually tall, light-skinned, with long flowing black hair and piercing eyes -- wearing a wide-brimmed hat and a flowing white, black, or red dress that conceals her horrifying secret: one leg ends in a cloven cow hoof instead of a human foot. She waits by the roadside at night, particularly near bridges, crossroads, and remote forest paths, and bewitches men (especially those returning from dances or rum shops) with her beauty and perfume. Once she lures a man deep into the forest, she reveals her true form and leads him to his doom -- into a ravine, a river, quicksand, or a cliff. Some say she drinks their blood; others say she simply laughs and vanishes, leaving the man hopelessly lost. She is a cautionary figure, warning against infidelity, lust, and wandering alone at night
source: Trinidadian oral tradition, Trinidad and Tobago folklore

name: La Garita del Diablo (The Devil's Sentry Box)
description: La Garita del Diablo (The Devil Sentry Box) is the most famous supernatural legend of Old San Juan, Puerto Rico. The story centers on a solitary sentry box (garita) at Castillo San Cristobal, perched on a rocky cliff above the crashing Atlantic. In the late 1600s, a Spanish soldier named Sanchez, nicknamed Flor de Azahar (Orange Blossom) for his pale white skin, was assigned to the farthest, most isolated sentry box. Sanchez was known for his beautiful guitar playing and his forbidden love for Diana, a local mestiza woman. One night, after the customary watchman calls echoed between the fort sentry boxes, Sanchez voice fell silent. At dawn, his fellow soldiers found his rifle, cartridge pouch, and uniform neatly folded inside the garita -- but Sanchez himself had vanished without a trace. Superstitious soldiers whispered that the devil had taken him. The true story, according to folklore, is that Diana brought him civilian clothes and they eloped together into the Luquillo Mountains. Yet to this day, visitors claim to hear the strumming of a guitar and soft laughter at the Garita del Diablo on windy nights
source: Puerto Rican oral tradition, Puerto Rico folklore

name: La Lechuza
description: La Lechuza is a terrifying shapeshifting witch from Mexican and Texas border folklore who transforms into a giant owl — seven feet tall with a fifteen-foot wingspan and the face of an old woman. According to legend, she was once a human woman who made a pact with the devil or practiced black magic, gaining the power to become an enormous owl that hunts at night. She preys primarily on drunk men and children, luring victims by mimicking the cry of a human infant or whistling. Her eyes glow like coals in the darkness, and her screech is said to be a death omen. In some versions, she is a witch's familiar serving an evil mistress; snip in others, a wronged mother seeking revenge on those who killed her child. Stories of La Lechuza are particularly widespread in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas and the Mexican states of Tamaulipas, Coahuila, Nuevo León, and Chihuahua
source: Mexican-American/Tejano folklore — La Lechuza the owl witch documented in Southwestern oral tradition.

name: La Llorona (The Weeping Woman)
description: ONE OF THE MOST FAMOUS Latin American ghosts — La Llorona ('The Weeping Woman') has pre-Columbian roots in the Aztec goddess Cihuacóatl, who appeared before the Spanish conquest weeping for the fate of her people. During the colonial period, the story syncretized with Spanish folklore of white ladies and became associated with La Malinche, Cortés's interpreter who bore his child — cursed by her people for betraying the Aztec Empire, condemned to wander forever weeping for her mestizo children. In the classic colonial version, a beautiful woman named María discovers her husband's infidelity, drowns her two children in a river, then drowns herself in grief. She now wanders eternally near water, wailing '¡Ay, mis hijos!' In the South Texas borderlands along the Rio Grande, Mexican-American communities tell of La Llorona appearing near irrigation canals and arroyos — sometimes as a protector warning mothers of danger rather than a predator. In New Mexico, the spirits of her drowned children appear as translucent figures playing near rivers at dusk. Chicana feminist writers like Gloria Anzaldúa and Sandra Cisneros have reclaimed La Llorona as a symbol of resistance, survival, and the power of the marginalized feminine voice
source: Latin American folklore; the Weeping Woman is a widespread ghost figure mourning her children.

name: La Loba
description: La Loba (The Wolf Woman) is a figure from New Mexican and Chicano folklore who protects the wild places and animals of the Southwestern desert. Older than any human, she is the guardian of wolf and coyote spirits. It is said that when a wolf dies, La Loba collects its bones and sings over them until the animal is reborn. She is described as an ancient woman who lives in a cave in the mountains, surrounded by the skulls and bones of animals. Children who get lost in the desert are said to be guided home by her, and hunters who kill for sport rather than need find their guns mysteriously jammed. The figure was popularized by Clarissa Pinkola Estés in her book 'Women Who Run With the Wolves,' which linked La Loba to the archetype of the wild feminine. In Chicano folklore, La Loba represents the deep connection between Hispanic peoples and the land of the Southwest, the wisdom of curanderas, and the power of women as healers and protectors of nature. Her legend connects to the nahual tradition of shapeshifting, as La Loba is sometimes said to transform between human and wolf form
source: Mexican-American/Southwestern folklore — La Loba wolf woman documented in Hispanic oral tradition.

name: La Mano Pachona
description: La Mano Pachona is a chilling legend from northern Mexico and the US Southwest about a disembodied, hairy hand that attacks travelers at night. The hand is described as large, dark, and covered in thick hair, with long fingernails. It wanders along lonely roads, scratching at windows and car doors, or reaches up from beneath vehicles to grab unsuspecting victims. Some versions claim the hand belongs to a man who was cursed for his evil deeds, while others say it is the hand of a murdered criminal that continues to seek revenge. In Mexican-American folklore of Texas and California, the story is often told around campfires and at sleepovers, serving as a tale of warning about traveling alone at night. La Mano Pachona represents the fear of the fragmented, disembodied threat — danger that comes not from a whole being but from something partial and inexplicable. The legend taps into the primal fear of being touched or grabbed from below or behind in the dark
source: Mexican folklore — La Mano Pachona spirit documented in Mexican oral tradition.

name: La Planchada
description: La Planchada (The Ironed One, referring to her perfectly pressed nurse's uniform) is a ghost legend from Mexico City hospitals that has spread through Mexican-American communities in the US Southwest. According to the story, a beautiful nurse named Eulalia worked at Hospital Juárez in the 1930s, deeply dedicated to her patients. She fell in love with a handsome doctor who courted her but ultimately abandoned her to marry another woman. Heartbroken, Eulalia died of sorrow, but her ghost now returns to the hospital where she once worked. Dressed in an immaculately starched white nurse's uniform, La Planchada appears in hospital wards at night, administering medicines, adjusting blankets, and comforting patients. Some patients claim to have recovered miraculously after being visited by her, while others say she only appears to those who are about to die. A key warning states that if you see the hem of her dress or her feet, you will die within days — a version of the classic 'don't look at their feet' motif. La Planchada has been reported in Mexican-American hospitals and clinics along the border, where she is viewed as a benevolent guardian spirit of the sick and dying
source: Mexican folklore — La Planchada ghost documented in Mexican hospital folklore.

name: La Siguanaba
description: A BEAUTIFUL WOMAN spirit from Mesoamerican folklore, particularly prevalent in El Salvador, Guatemala, and southern Mexico, with variants told in Mexican-American communities of the US Southwest. The legend has pre-Columbian origins among the Pipil and Maya peoples, where female water spirits were associated with both fertility and danger. La Siguanaba appears as a stunningly beautiful woman with long, flowing hair, seen bathing in rivers or washing clothes. She lures men — especially those who are unfaithful or have been drinking — by appearing as their lover or a beautiful stranger. When the man approaches, she transforms, revealing her true face: that of a horse or a skull, driving him mad with terror. Some versions say she then attacks and kills him. The name derives from the Nahuatl 'cihuatl' (woman) and may be related to Aztec Cihuacóatl. In the US Southwest, the story is told among Chicano communities as a warning against infidelity, drunkenness, and the dangers of trusting appearances — particularly to young men who stray from their commitments
source: Central American folklore; a shape-shifting female spirit who lures men near water.

name: Lạc Long Quân (Dragon Lord of Lạc)
description: Lạc Long Quân (literally 'Dragon Lord of Lạc') is the legendary dragon king and founding ancestor of the Vietnamese people. Son of Kinh Dương Vương and the sea goddess Long Nữ, he ruled the Lạc Việt people along the rivers and coast of what is now northern Vietnam. He taught the Lạc Việt to cultivate wet rice, cook food, and tattoo their bodies with sea-dragon designs so ocean creatures would recognize them. He married the mountain fairy Âu Cơ, and from their union came an egg sac that hatched one hundred children — the ancestors of the Vietnamese nation. As a being of water and sea, he eventually separated from Âu Cơ (a being of the mountains), taking fifty children to the coast while she took fifty to the highlands. Their eldest son became the first Hùng King, founding the Hồng Bàng dynasty. Lạc Long Quân is revered as the father of Vietnamese civilization
source: Vietnamese myth, Lĩnh Nam chích quái (14th century), Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư

name: Ladejarlens Gjenferd
description: Ladejarlens Gjenferd (the Ghost of the Lade Jarl) is a spectral figure said to haunt the Lade area of Trondheim, where the powerful Lade Jarls had their seat in the Viking Age and early Middle Ages. The Lade Jarls (Earls of Lade) ruled much of Norway from their base at Lade (modern-day Trondheim) from the 9th to 11th centuries. The most famous of them — Håkon Grjotgardsson, Håkon Sigurdsson, and Eirik Håkonsson — were among the most powerful men in Norse history. Their ghost is said to appear as a tall, armored figure riding a spectral horse along the old road from Lade to the Nidelva river. The apparition is seen most often on stormy winter nights, sometimes accompanied by the sounds of battle. The legend reflects the lingering presence of Norway's Viking Age rulers in the Trondheim landscape, where their power once shaped the nation's history
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: La Diablesse
description: In Saint Lucia, La Diablesse is a beautiful white demoness usually encountered on bridges or near rivers. She will talk quietly and politely to her victim before using her magical beauty to lure him into the forest. Once enchanted, the victim will be fed on lizards, wood ants, and snakes. Sometimes he is never seen again; if he is lucky, he will awake the next morning in a crevice on some rockface or ravine. She can be recognized by her cloven foot and by the heavy steel fetters glimpsed under her skirts. Making the sign of the cross will make a true Diablesse immediately disappear. Saint Lucian folklorist Kennedy Boot Samuel has documented how the Diablesse legend is still whispered about in rural communities. The legend likely blends French colonial devil imagery with West African spirit concepts, creating a uniquely Saint Lucian cautionary figure about the dangers of temptation
source: Dominican oral tradition; snip DOM767 Dominican Folklore; snip Wikipedia

name: La Diablesse
description: In Saint Lucia, La Diablesse is a beautiful white demoness usually encountered on bridges or near rivers. She will talk quietly and politely to her victim before using her magical beauty to lure him into the forest. Once enchanted, the victim will be fed on lizards, wood ants, and snakes. Sometimes he is never seen again; if he is lucky, he will awake the next morning in a crevice on some rockface or ravine. She can be recognized by her cloven foot and by the heavy steel fetters glimpsed under her skirts. Making the sign of the cross will make a true Diablesse immediately disappear. Saint Lucian folklorist Kennedy Boot Samuel has documented how the Diablesse legend is still whispered about in rural communities. The legend likely blends French colonial devil imagery with West African spirit concepts, creating a uniquely Saint Lucian cautionary figure about the dangers of temptation In Saint Lucia folklore, this figure is known among the Saint Lucian Creole people.
source: Saint Lucian oral tradition; snip The Independent (1996); snip Wikipedia

name: Lamia (Λάμια)
description: The Lamia is a child-devouring female monster deeply embedded in Greek Cypriot folklore, descended from the ancient Lamia of Greek mythology who was cursed by Hera to eat children. In Cypriot tradition, she is a solitary, nocturnal creature who dwells in caves and remote mountain passes, preying on children who wander too far from home. She is said to have the ability to remove her own eyes, which she places in a bowl to sleep — if someone steals her eyes, she becomes blind and helpless until she gets them back. This motif appears in many Cypriot folktales collected in the Troodos villages. The Lamia is also associated with desolate places, old ruins, and deserted wells. Mothers in rural Cyprus, particularly in villages like Kakopetria and Platres, would threaten disobedient children with the Lamia to keep them close to home. In some versions, she is a shape-shifter who can appear as a beautiful woman to lure men before revealing her true horrific form
source: Greek mythology, Hesiod & Homer

name: Landvættir
description: Landvættir (land wights) are the four guardian spirits of Iceland described in Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla. Each guardian protects one quarter of Iceland's coast: a dragon (gríðungur) guards the east, a giant eagle or griffin (gammur) guards the north, a bull (griðungur) guards the west, and a rock giant (bergrisi) guards the south. According to the legend, King Harald Gormsson of Denmark sent a wizard in whale-form to scout Iceland for invasion. The wizard tried to land on each coast but was driven away by the four landvættir — the dragon breathed fire, the eagle tore at his eyes, the bull charged with horns, and the giant smashed him with a club. The wizard returned to Denmark and reported that Iceland could not be conquered. The landvættir are depicted on Iceland's coat of arms and on Icelandic króna coins. They represent the protective power of the Icelandic landscape itself
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Lekamøya
description: Lekamøya (the Leka Maid) is a female troll figure from Nordland folklore, serving as the nanny of the Seven Sisters — the daughters of Suliskongen. According to the legend cycle, when Hestmannen pursued the Seven Sisters, Lekamøya tried to protect them. She fled south from the horseman, leaping across Velfjorden toward Leka island. As the sun rose, she was turned to stone mid-flight. The butter keg she was carrying fell from her hands and became the yellow-colored mountains on Leka island (which are geologically distinct — composed of ultramafic rock with a distinctive yellow-green color). The Lekamøya rock formation is clearly visible on Leka, one of the most famous rock formations in Nordland. The legend explains both the rock formation and the unusual geology of Leka. The island of Leka is located on the border between Trøndelag and Nordland
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: Leuk (Hare)
description: Leuk is the clever hare trickster of Wolof folklore from Senegal, the embodiment of intelligence triumphing over brute force. In countless Wolof tales, Leuk uses his wit, cunning, and patience to overcome larger, stronger adversaries — most often Bouki the Hyena, who is greedy, foolish, and easily tricked. The Leuk-Bouki cycle is the most famous body of Wolof folklore, with Leuk consistently outwitting his larger companion. Leuk represents the Wolof cultural value that intelligence and cleverness are more valuable than physical strength. The character became widely known through the literary works of Léopold Sédar Senghor ("La Belle Histoire de Leuk le Lièvre") and Birago Diop ("Les Contes d'Amadou Koumba"). Leuk is the Wolof equivalent of Anansi the Spider in Akan culture or Brer Rabbit in African American folklore
source: Wolof folklore of Senegal — Leuk hare trickster documented in Senegalese oral traditions.

name: Álfar
description: Álfar (elves) are nature-dwelling spirits in Icelandic folklore, distinct from the Huldufólk (hidden people) in several key ways. While Huldufólk are considered to be human-like beings living in a parallel society, álfar are more ethereal, nature-bound beings associated with specific rocks, hills, and cliffs. In Icelandic tradition, álfar are beautiful, graceful, and possess magical powers. They live inside rocks (álfhólar — elf hills) and practice farming in parallel to human farmers. If offended, they can cause illness, misfortune, or accidents. If respected, they bring good luck. Offerings were traditionally left for the álfar at certain rocks. In Norse mythology, the álfar appear in the Poetic Edda and Snorra Edda as a distinct race. Kormáks saga mentions a sacrifice to álfar for healing. Modern Iceland still has a strong álfar belief tradition, with many Icelanders believing in their existence
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Lindesnes-varulven
description: Lindesnes-varulven (the werewolf of Lindesnes) is a shapeshifting wolf-creature from the folklore of the Lindesnes region, the southernmost tip of Norway. Unlike the continental European werewolf tradition, the Lindesnes-varulv is more closely related to Norse concepts of hamskifte (shape-shifting) — a person who could transform into a wolf by putting on a wolf-skin belt or by being born under a specific configuration of stars. The Lindesnes werewolf was documented in the Norsk Folkeminnesamling's national sagnkart (legend map) project launched in 2018, which mapped folk legends across Norway's municipalities. The Lindesnes variant is notable for being one of the few documented werewolf traditions in southern Norway — most Norwegian werewolf/lycanthrope traditions come from the central and northern regions. The Lindesnes-varulv was said to haunt the heath and coastal areas around the Lindesnes lighthouse, preying on livestock and lone travelers
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Lindorm
description: Lindormen is a giant serpentine dragon in Danish folklore, living under churches, in burial mounds, and in lakes. The most famous Danish Lindorm legend comes from Hvalsø Church in Sjælland, where a Lindorm once coiled itself around the entire church, preventing anyone from entering. The beast was defeated by a special bull raised on milk and hazelnuts — the bull charged and disemboweled the Lindorm in a ravine that is still called 'Tyvedskløften' (Bull's Gully). In Danish tradition, Lindormer are associated with curses — some legends tell of princes transformed into Lindormer (the 'King Lindorm' tale type ATU 433B), who can only be restored to human form by a princess brave enough to embrace the serpent. Unlike dragons, the Danish Lindorm has no wings and breathes poison rather than fire In Denmark folklore, this figure is known among the Denmark people.
source: Germanic/Nordic folklore; the Lindorm is a wingless serpentine dragon.

name: Liongo Fumo
description: Liongo Fumo (also known as Fumo Liyongo) is the national hero of the Swahili people -- a legendary warrior, poet, and prince who lived on Pate Island (Lamu Archipelago) sometime between the 9th and 13th centuries. A giant of a man, nearly invulnerable except for his navel, a master archer whose bow no other man could draw, and a poet of such skill that his compositions survive as the oldest known Swahili literature. Though the rightful heir, his brother Mringwari usurped the throne, forcing Liongo into exile. He became a heroic outlaw, composing poems and songs still sung at weddings and gungu dances. His death came through betrayal -- his own son stabbed him in the navel with a copper needle. Mortally wounded, Liongo staggered to a well, dying upright with his bow in hand, so fearsome that none dared approach until his mother confirmed his passing
source: Swahili oral tradition, Alice Werner 'Myths and Legends of the Bantu', Jan Knappert, Wikipedia

name: Listasanddjevelen
description: Listasanddjevelen (the Sand Devil of Lista) is a supernatural being associated with the shifting sand dunes of the Lista peninsula in Sørlandet. Lista has one of Norway's most dramatic dune landscapes — the Listastrendene beaches with massive moving sand dunes that have buried farms, roads, and churches over the centuries. The sand devil was believed to be a spirit that controlled the movement of the dunes, causing them to shift and bury farmland, buildings, and travelers caught in sandstorms. Local tradition said the sand devil had to be appeased with offerings to prevent the dunes from advancing. The sand devil reflects the real environmental challenge of sand drift on Lista — a problem that plagued the region from the 1600s until modern dune stabilization efforts. The spirit could be seen on stormy nights, a whirling figure of sand and wind moving across the dunes
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Lungu (The Great Snake)
description: Lungu is a mythical great snake from Zambian folklore, particularly among the Bemba people, believed to inhabit the underworld and to have power over rain and fertility. Unlike the more localized Chitapo and Funkwe, Lungu is a broader, more elemental figure whose domain extends across the entire region. The great snake is associated with the creation of rivers and lakes, and is believed to control weather patterns and influence the growth of crops. Farmers and villagers traditionally perform rituals to appease Lungu, asking for rain and bountiful harvests. The myth underscores the deep connection between Zambian communities and their natural environment, particularly the dependence on rainfall for agriculture in a region where drought can be devastating. Lungu is said to travel between water sources through underground passages, and his movements are believed to cause earthquakes and the formation of new springs. In some versions, Lungu is a primordial being who carried the first humans across the great waters on his back, making him both a creator and a sustainer of life
source: Youth Village Zambia; Bemba oral traditions

name: Lunja
description: Lunja (also Loundja) is a central female figure in Kabyle (Algerian Amazigh) mythology, the beautiful daughter of the ogress Teryel. In traditional tellings, Lunja is described as a maiden of extraordinary beauty — white skin, olive-shaped eyes, long black shining hair — who lives as a captive in her mother's cave. Initially portrayed as passive and silent, scholarly re-examination (particularly from feminist perspectives) has revealed Lunja as a complex trickster figure who uses silence, clever speech, and strategic submission to navigate her mother's tyranny and ultimately achieve freedom. In one famous episode, she tricks the river spirit into letting her cross by claiming Teryel is chasing her. When heroes come to rescue her, she negotiates terms that benefit her while maintaining the appearance of obedience. Lunja represents the Kabyle woman's strategies of survival and resistance within a patriarchal structure — using wit, indirection, and performed submission as tools of liberation. She is sometimes compared to the Greek Psyche figure and appears in tales across Algeria and the wider Maghreb
source: Frobenius collection; Lacoste-Dujardin; Henri Basset; Sinestesieonline academic journal; Kabyle oral traditions

name: Lussi
description: Lussi is a female demon-like figure in Norwegian folklore active on Lussinatten (St. Lucy's Night, December 13), one of the shortest days of the year in the old Julian calendar. On this night, Lussi rides through the air with a host of spirits and demons, punishing anyone who dared to work after dark. All spinning wheels and looms had to be still. Anyone caught working risked being swept up by Lussi's procession or having their work ruined. In Vestlandet, the Lussinatten tradition was particularly strong — no mill could operate, no wool could be spun, and no bread could be baked after sunset. Lussi also punished children who misbehaved. The tradition merged with St. Lucy's Day (Santa Lucia) celebrations after Christianization, but Lussi herself remained a feared figure in rural folklore centuries after. The night was considered extremely dangerous — even animals could speak on Lussinatten, though hearing them meant death for the listener
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Lyktemann
description: Lyktemann (lantern-man), also known as lyktgubbe, is a will-o'-the-wisp ghost light in Norwegian folklore particularly associated with the marshlands and coastal bogs of Vestlandet. The lyktemann appears as a small, dancing light that leads travelers astray into dangerous marshes, bogs, or cliffs. Following the light means certain death — the victim either drowns in a bog or falls from a cliff. The light could not be caught or approached — it always stayed just ahead. In some traditions, the lyktemann is the ghost of a sinful person condemned to wander with a lantern for eternity. Regional variations: in Hordaland it is called lyktemann, in Sogn it is vettelys (spirit light). Some fishermen along the Vestlandet coast believed the lyktemann was a warning of death at sea — seeing one near the shore meant a family member would drown
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Lyngbakr
description: Lyngbakr (Heather-Back) is the largest whale in Icelandic folklore, so massive that its back looks like a heather-covered island covered in soil, grass, and small trees. Sailors would land on what they thought was an island only to discover they had landed on Lyngbakr's back. When the whale submerged, the sailors would drown. Lyngbakr appears in Örvar-Odds saga and the Navigatio Sancti Brendani (Saint Brendan's Voyage). The name comes from lyng (heather) and bak (back). According to the legend, Lyngbakr is the second-largest sea creature after only Hafgufa. It feeds only once every three years, opening its enormous mouth to engulf everything in its path. Lyngbakr was believed to live until Ragnarök. The legend likely originated from sightings of whale backs or floating debris fields mistaken for islands
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Møllergut
description: Møllergut (mill boy) is a milder, more helpful mill spirit in Norwegian folklore, counterpart to the malicious kvernknurr. The møllergut is a young apprentice spirit who helps the miller with his work — cleaning the millstones, carrying sacks of grain, and keeping the mill race clear of debris. Unlike the kvernknurr who deliberately breaks the mill, the møllergut assists if treated kindly. He expects small offerings — a bowl of porridge left in the mill at night, or a piece of flatbread. If neglected, he becomes mischievous rather than truly destructive — hiding the miller's hat, switching grain sacks, or making strange noises. The møllergut is particularly associated with the smaller farm mills of Vestlandet where a single miller worked alone at night. He represents the more benign, childlike spirits of Norwegian folk belief
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Mae Phosop (Rice Goddess)
description: Mae Phosop (Lao: ແມ່ໂພສົບ, Thai: แม่โพสพ, 'Mother of the Rice Kernel') is the ancient rice goddess revered in Lao, Thai, and Isan agricultural traditions. According to legend, she was a beautiful celestial maiden who descended to earth to become the spirit of rice — the essence that sustains all life. In primordial times, rice grew as large as pumpkins and flew directly into granaries by itself. However, a careless woman struck a rice kernel with her broom in anger, and the offended rice spirit withdrew into hiding, causing famine. The people had to perform elaborate ceremonies to call Mae Phosop back. Today, before planting, farmers perform the 'Rice Mother Calling' ritual (riak khwan khao), offering bananas, sugarcane, and flowers. At harvest, the most beautiful rice stalks are selected and dressed in silk as an offering. Mae Phosop teaches that rice is a living spiritual entity deserving of gratitude and respect — an animist belief that coexists with Theravada Buddhism throughout the Lao world
source: Lao and Isan agricultural tradition, Tai folk religion

name: Mae Yanang (Boat Guardian Spirit)
description: Mae Yanang (Thai: แม่ย่านาง) is a revered female guardian spirit who protects boats, vehicles, and travelers in Thai, Lao, and Khmer folk religion. She is believed to reside in the prow of every wooden boat, especially those made from Takhian wood (Hopea odorata), which was thought to house benevolent tree spirits. Fishermen and sailors perform elaborate ceremonies before voyages, offering flowers, incense, tricolor cloth, and food to invoke her protection. The prow of a boat decorated with colored sashes and garlands signals her presence. In modern times, belief in Mae Yanang has expanded to include cars, motorcycles, and even airplanes, with drivers offering garlands and incense at dashboards. Her worship derives from ancient matrifocal animist traditions and shares origins with Mae Phosop and Nang Kwak. She is distinctively propitiated at traffic lights throughout Thailand where vendors sell floral garlands to drivers
source: Thai folk religion, Tai animist traditions, Phraya Anuman Rajadhon ethnographic studies

name: Mahagiri Nat (Great Mountain Spirit)
description: Mahagiri Nat (Burmese: မဟာဂီရိနတ်, 'Great Mountain Spirit') is one of the most powerful nats in the Burmese pantheon, the guardian of homes and protector against fires. According to legend, he was originally a mighty blacksmith named Nga Tin De (or Nga Tin Te) who forged weapons of unparalleled quality in the village of Taungbyon. King Thinligyawng of Tagaung, fearing the blacksmith's power, summoned him to the capital and had him burned alive inside a champaca tree. Nga Tin De's sister threw herself into the flames to die beside him, and their spirits were trapped in the tree, terrorizing the region. When King Anawrahta cut down the tree, he ordered the spirits carved into statues and enshrined — the male spirit became Mahagiri Nat, installed at the gates of Pagan's royal palace, while the female became Popa Medaw on Mount Popa. Mahagiri Nat is now the guardian spirit of all Burmese homes, traditionally enshrined at the southeast corner of the house compound
source: Burmese nat religion — Mahagiri Great Mountain nat.

name: Makonde Witchcraft Spirits (Uchawi)
description: The Makonde people of northern Mozambique have a highly developed tradition of witchcraft and sorcery (uchawi) that involves a complex hierarchy of spirits and practitioners. In Makonde cosmology, witchcraft spirits are believed to be deployed by both malevolent individuals and traditional healers to achieve various ends. These spirits are distinct from the more generalized shetani in that they are specifically associated with human practitioners who use them for targeted purposes. Magic plays an influential role in Makonde culture, politics, and economics. Witchcraft can be used for both harmful purposes (causing illness, death, or misfortune) and protective purposes (defending against attacks, ensuring harvests). The Makonde distinguish between different types of witchcraft: inherited witchcraft (passed down family lines), learned sorcery (studied through apprenticeship), and spirit-induced witchcraft (where a spirit chooses a person). Accusations of witchcraft have serious social consequences and are adjudicated by traditional courts. The belief system provides explanations for misfortune and maintains social order through the fear of supernatural retribution
source: Wikipedia (Makonde witchcraft and sorcery)

name: Malin Kundang
description: Malin Kundang is the tragic protagonist of West Sumatra's most famous folktale, a cautionary story about filial ingratitude. A poor boy from a fishing village, Malin Kundang leaves his widowed mother to seek fortune overseas. After years of hardship, he becomes a wealthy merchant, marries a princess, and returns home in a grand ship. His elderly mother, overjoyed, rushes to embrace him, but Malin Kundang, ashamed of his humble origins in front of his wife and crew, cruelly denies knowing her and orders her driven away. Heartbroken, his mother kneels and prays to God to punish her ungrateful son. A violent storm immediately strikes, and Malin Kundang and his ship are turned to stone. The stone ship remains visible on the coast of Air Manis Beach in Padang, West Sumatra, as a permanent warning against filial disrespect
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malin_Kundang

name: Maman Brigitte (Queen of the Cemetery)
description: Maman Brigitte is the powerful female lwa of death, cemeteries, and the underworld in Haitian Vodou. She is the wife of Baron Samedi, the master of the dead, and together they rule the Gede family of spirits. She is depicted as a pale-skinned woman with long red or black hair, dressed in black and purple mourning clothes, often wearing a black veil and carrying a broom or shovel. She is fiercely protective of graves and ancestors, and those who defile a cemetery risk her terrible wrath. Despite her macabre domain, she is also a maternal figure who offers comfort to the grieving and protects the souls of the dead. Maman Brigitte is syncretized with Saint Brigid of Ireland, a fascinating example of Celtic-Caribbean syncretism brought by Irish indentured servants in colonial Haiti. Her colors are black, purple, and deep red. Her offerings include black coffee, dark rum infused with hot peppers, and black hens sacrificed at crossroads near cemeteries
source: Haitian Vodou oral tradition, Haiti folklore

name: Mannbjørn
description: Mannbjørn (man-bear) is a werebear in Norwegian folklore — a human who can transform into a bear. In Norwegian tradition, the bear transformation was more common than the werewolf of continental European folklore. The mannbjørn could transform by putting on a bearskin, by drinking a magical potion, or through a family curse. While in bear form, the person retained human intelligence but gained the bear's strength and ferocity. Vestlandet legends tell of men who became bears to fight enemies, protect their farms, or survive in the wilderness. Some mannbjørn were cursed to transform during the winter months and could only be freed if someone recognized them. Unlike the berserkir of the Viking Age (who fought in a trance-like state), the mannbjørn physically transformed. The tradition was particularly strong in the remote mountain valleys of Vestlandet where brown bears were common until the 19th century
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.
